Exophthalmometry was R 15 mm—112 mm—L 16 mm. Slit lamp examination showed an intact right globe. The crystalline lens was clear in both eyes, and the vitreous was quiet. Dilated fundus examination showed no abnormality to the left eye, however a raised white retinal lesion was noted in the right eye, superior-temporal to the optic disc approximately 4-disc diameters away and approximately 1.5-disc diameters in length

report.source_text: Once the patient was stabilized, follow up examinations for the tripod fracture were arranged by the Maxillofacial department with Ophthalmology input requested to investigate the possibility of a retained IOFB, given the hyperattenuating lesion noted in the right eye on CT imaging (Fig. 1).Fig. 1(A) Axial CT showing a hyperdense lesion in the right eye (red arrow). (B) CT scan of his face, which was done at the time of the accident, showed a right sided tripod fracture involving the right orbital floor, zygomatic arch and maxillary sinuses (yellow arrows). There is blood in the right maxillary sinus (x). A hyper-dense lesion is noted in the right eye on CT which raises the possibility of a retained IOFB (red arrow).Fig 1 Background ocular history includes bilateral keratoconus, with a previous 3 right penetrating keratoplasties, with moderate keratoconus remaining in the left eye, predominantly managed with a rigid gas permeable lens. Unaided visual acuity of the right eye was counting fingers improving to 6/15 with pinhole, left eye aided visual acuity was 6/7.5 with a rigid contact lens in-situ. Intraocular pressures were RE 10 mmHg and LE 6 mmHg. Eye movements were full and unrestricted in both eyes. Color plate testing with Ishihara was full and brisk in each eye. Monocular confrontational visual field testing was clear of obvious abnormality in either eye. Pupils were equal and reactive to light with no sign of relative afferent pupillary defect. Exophthalmometry was R 15 mm—112 mm—L 16 mm. Slit lamp examination showed an intact right globe. The right corneal graft was reasonably clear with no sign of rejection or dehiscence, whilst the left cornea showed signs of moderate keratoconus. Both anterior chambers were deep and quiet. The crystalline lens was clear in both eyes, and the vitreous was quiet. Dilated fundus examination showed no abnormality to the left eye, however a raised white retinal lesion was noted in the right eye, superior-temporal to the optic disc approximately 4-disc diameters away and approximately 1.5-disc diameters in length (Fig. 2)Fig. 2Optos image of the patient's right fundus. Highlighted is a white, raised retinal lesion superotemporal to the right optic nerve head.Fig 2 Enhanced depth optical coherence tomography (EDI-OCT) imaging through the right retinal lesion was obtained (Fig. 3) which shows a typical double “rocky and rolling” elevation with no sign of subretinal fluid or detachment.Fig. 3OCT through the right retinal lesion which shows a typical double "rocky and rolling" elevation with no subretinal fluid.Fig 3

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 41-year-old New Zealand European male with a history of bilateral keratoconus and three prior right penetrating keratoplasties sustained a car vs bicycle collision with ejection, resulting in a right tripod facial fracture (involving orbital floor, zygomatic arch, and maxillary sinuses) and multiple other injuries. Initial CT imaging revealed a hyperattenuating lesion in the right eye that raised concern for a retained intraocular foreign body (IOFB). Ophthalmology evaluation documented an intact right globe with a clear corneal graft, normal anterior and posterior segments, full eye movements, normal pupils, normal visual fields, and normal color vision. Dilated fundus examination revealed a raised white retinal lesion located superior-temporal to the optic disc, approximately 4-disc diameters away and 1.5-disc diameters in length. Enhanced depth optical coherence tomography (EDI-OCT) imaging through the lesion demonstrated a characteristic double 'rocky and rolling' elevation pattern with no subretinal fluid or detachment. This OCT appearance is pathognomonic for choroidal calcification. The clinical and imaging findings established that the hyperattenuating lesion on CT and the white raised retinal lesion represented a benign scleral-choroidal calcification at the superior oblique insertion, not a traumatic retained foreign body. No globe injury was identified.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Intact globe on clinical examination, characteristic 'rocky and rolling' OCT elevation pattern pathognomonic for choroidal calcification rather than foreign material, absence of subretinal fluid or detachment, normal eye movements and visual function
Slit lamp examination documented intact right globe with clear corneal graft and no sign of dehiscence
EDI-OCT imaging showed no subretinal fluid or detachment

remaining_uncertainties: Explicit documentation of the lesion location at the superior oblique insertion (inferred from final diagnosis statement but not directly confirmed in accessible clinical documentation)
Detailed radiological explanation of why the hyperattenuating CT appearance is consistent with benign calcification rather than metallic foreign body
Whether additional imaging modalities (B-scan ultrasound, MRI) were performed to further characterize the lesion

final.final_diagnosis: Right unilateral scleral choroidal calcification at the site of the superior oblique insertion with no globe injury related to the trauma
